title: Complaint Handling
blurb: How to listen, take ownership and follow through when a guest complains, and which complaints go straight to the Duty Manager.
siteNotes: Who the Duty Manager is on each shift and how to reach them quickly
What staff are allowed to put right themselves (for example replacing a dish) before a manager is needed
legalNotes: From BHB-10MT-21. Guest-service good practice; no specific regulation is stated in the trainer.

CHECK: the trainer says research "consistently shows" a well-handled complaint can leave a guest more loyal. This is a widely quoted service-recovery finding, but the trainer gives no source, and the slides state it without citing a study.

CHECK: allergic reactions, illness and injury must go to the Duty Manager; confirm the venue also expects these to be recorded (accident book, allergen incident log) after the guest has been looked after.

cards.title: Complaint Handling
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- explain why a complaint is a chance, not a problem
- listen, apologise and take ownership
- know which complaints go straight to the Duty Manager

cards.title: A complaint is a gift
cards.body:
A guest who complains is giving us the chance to put things right. A complaint handled well often leaves a guest **more loyal** than if nothing had gone wrong.
> The guests to worry about are the ones who say nothing and never come back.

items.title: Speaks up
items.text: We get the chance to fix it

items.title: Says nothing
items.text: We never find out; they do not return

cards.title: Listen first
cards.body: Listening is the first and most important skill. Give the guest your full attention and let them finish. Do not get defensive or make excuses. Often people just want to feel heard.

cards.title: Apologise without blame
cards.body:
Acknowledge how the guest feels and apologise for the experience. You can be genuinely sorry that someone's evening was spoiled without arguing about who is to blame.
> Never argue with a guest. Never discuss whose fault it was in front of them or other diners.

cards.title: Take ownership
cards.body: If you can put it right, do it. If it is beyond you, do not pass the buck: escalate it to a manager promptly and make sure the guest knows it is being taken seriously.

items.title: Apologise
items.text: For the experience, not the blame

items.title: Follow through
items.text: Agree next steps, then thank them

cards.kicker: Go straight to the Duty Manager
cards.title: Urgent complaints
cards.body: Agree what happens next, follow through and thank the guest for raising it. Some issues are urgent and must go straight to the Duty Manager.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- A complaint is a chance to put things right.
- Listen first and let them finish. No excuses.
- Apologise for the experience. Never argue or blame in front of guests.
- Fix it or escalate promptly, then follow through and say thank you.
- Allergic reaction, illness, injury or legal or online threats: Duty Manager at once.

cards.q: A complaint handled well can leave a guest more loyal than before.
cards.why: A well-handled complaint often leaves a guest more loyal than if nothing had gone wrong.

cards.q: What is the first and most important skill in handling a complaint?
options: Offering a refund as soon as they speak
Listening, giving full attention until they finish
Explaining how the mistake came about
Telling them it will not happen again
cards.why: Listening comes first. Often people simply want to feel heard.

cards.q: When a guest is complaining you should…
options: Interrupt to explain
Walk away
Ask a colleague to take over
Listen and let them finish
cards.why: Give your full attention and let them finish without interrupting.

cards.q: You can apologise for a guest's experience without arguing about blame.
cards.why: You can be genuinely sorry someone's evening was spoiled without arguing about who is to blame.

cards.q: If you can't resolve a complaint yourself, you should…
options: Ignore it and hope it passes
Argue your case until they accept
Escalate it to a manager promptly
Tell the guest to write in later
cards.why: Do not pass the buck. Escalate promptly and make sure the guest knows it is being taken seriously.

cards.q: It's fine to discuss whose fault it was in front of the guest.
cards.why: Never discuss whose fault it was in front of the guest or other diners.

cards.q: Which of these must go straight to the Duty Manager?
options: A guest says the soup was lukewarm
A guest says the music is too loud
A guest says the wait for a table was long
A guest threatens to post about it online
cards.why: Allergic reactions, illness, injury and any threat of legal or online action go straight to the Duty Manager.

cards.q: The guests to really worry about are those who say nothing and don't return.
cards.why: Guests who stay silent give us no chance to put things right, and they simply do not come back.

cards.q: After resolving a complaint you should…
options: Say nothing and move on quickly
Add a charge for the trouble
Follow through and thank the guest
Ask them to leave a review online
cards.why: Agree what happens next, follow through on it and thank them for raising it.

cards.q: Getting defensive and making excuses is a good way to handle a complaint.
cards.why: Do not get defensive or make excuses. Listen, acknowledge and take ownership.
